stimulus.text: The cartoon shows a classroom. A teacher, tied with ropes and gagged, points with a stick at a wall chart titled “MAP OF THE EARTH.” The chart shows a flat strip of land marked “AMERICA,” “BRITISH ISLES,” “EUROPE,” and “ASIA,” with the space below it labeled “VOID.” A framed portrait labeled “PREXY” hangs on the wall, and a second chart labeled “HELL” shows flames. Two students watch from desks below. The caption reads: “CLASSROOM IN PROPOSED BRYAN UNIVERSITY OF TENNESSEE.” — Rollin Kirby, 1925.
stimulus.source_note: Rollin Kirby, “Classroom in Proposed Bryan University of Tennessee,” 1925. Public domain (published 1925, pre-1930); via Wikimedia Commons.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Rollin Kirby cartoon, 1925, public domain
stem: The gagged teacher in the cartoon best supports which claim about the Scopes trial era?

options.text: Tennessee lawmakers wanted more science taught in schools
options.misconception: Tennessee passed a law against teaching evolution. Lawmakers wanted less science in schools, not more.

options.text: most Americans agreed that evolution was true by then
options.misconception: The trial drew national attention because Americans disagreed deeply. Agreement would have made no trial at all.

options.text: defenders of traditional religion used state power against science
the trial settled the debate over evolution for good
options.misconception: The debate went on long after 1925. One trial did not settle how Americans thought about science and religion.

rationales.A: Tennessee passed a law against teaching evolution. Lawmakers wanted less science in schools, not more.
rationales.B: The trial drew national attention because Americans disagreed deeply. Agreement would have made no trial at all.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Tennessee's Butler Act made teaching evolution a crime, and Scopes was tried for breaking it. The gagged teacher shows the law working as its supporters meant it to work.
rationales.D: The debate went on long after 1925. One trial did not settle how Americans thought about science and religion.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the gag means: the teacher is stopped from speaking.
2. Ask who stopped him: a state law. Background: Tennessee's Butler Act made teaching evolution a crime, and Bryan backed it.
3. Ask what the law stopped: teaching evolution, the new science.
4. Name the pattern: traditional belief defended by state power against new science.
Remember: when a cartoon shows a person silenced, ask who did the silencing and what was silenced.
